clue.text: Occupy London captures a tower

indicators.note: captures says the phrase Occupy London holds the answer within its run of letters

parts.note: the answer is the tail of occupy joined to the start of London

explanation.surface: Protesters from the Occupy movement in London take over a tower.
explanation.walkthrough: Occupy London was the 2011 protest camp beside St Paul's Cathedral; the answer straddles the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A pylon is a tall steel structure carrying power lines, a kind of tower.

clue.text: Sprinkles phosphorus ray — an occupational hazard?

parts.note: to pepper is to sprinkle or scatter over
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chemistry-lab hazard of sprinkled phosphorus and radiation.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark puns on occupation: police used pepper spray on Occupy protesters in 2011.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepper spray was the irritant used against protesters, a hazard of taking part in an Occupy encampment.

clue.text: Greener pasture diverted fire

parts.note: a lea is a meadow or pasture

indicators.note: diverted means the word fire is sent off course, its letters rearranged

parts.note: the four letters of fire are the ones rearranged

explanation.surface: A fire on the other side of the fence is turned away from greener grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Greener can mean having more foliage, which is what leafier says.

clue.text: Tear into wine ad throughout the magazine?

indicators.note: tear means rip apart, so the letters of into wine ad are pulled into a new order

parts.note: these three words supply exactly the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone rips into a wine advert that appears throughout a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The magazine is The Nation, where the puzzle ran, so all through it is the answer, playfully.
explanation.definitionFit: Nationwide means across the whole country; the question mark reads it as across all of The Nation.

clue.text: Unoccupied resort town seized by a fit

indicators.note: seized by puts the resort town inside the phrase a fit, which grips it

parts.note: taken as written
able means fit, as in fit or able to work
Vail is a ski resort town in Colorado

explanation.surface: An empty holiday town is gripped by some seizure.
explanation.definitionFit: An unoccupied seat or room is free for use, which is what the answer means.

clue.text: Scared of air force incursion…

parts.note: AF is the standard abbreviation for air force
a raid is a sudden incursion into enemy ground

explanation.surface: People are frightened of an air strike.
explanation.definitionFit: Afraid and scared both describe feeling fear.

clue.text: …and one excellent baseball team

parts.note: swell is dated slang for excellent
the Oakland A's are a Major League Baseball team

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a fine baseball team joins in.
explanation.definitionFit: As well as adds one thing to another, the same job the conjunction and does.

clue.text: Songbird's amusing escapade

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small brown bird famous for singing in flight
second meaning: a bit of fun or mischief

explanation.surface: A bird's playful adventure.
explanation.definitionFit: The skylark is a songbird, and doing something for a lark means doing it for fun.

clue.text: What banks might get from taxpayers: trouble during an outbreak

definitions.text: What banks might get from taxpayers

indicators.note: during puts the trouble inside the outbreak, happening within it

parts.note: a bout is an outbreak, as in a bout of flu
to ail is to trouble

explanation.surface: A jab at bank rescues: taxpayers foot the bill when sickness strikes.
explanation.definitionFit: Banks rescued with public money in 2008 received a bailout from taxpayers.

clue.text: See 26 down
Stapler defaced wall's coating

indicators.note: defaced means the word stapler is spoiled and its letters disfigured into a new order

parts.note: the word stapler supplies the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone vandalised a stapler, and the wall's covering gets a mention too.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaster is the smooth layer spread over interior walls before painting.

clue.text: Message overwhelms Republican that is preoccupied

indicators.note: overwhelms means the message engulfs what follows, surrounding it completely

parts.note: word means a message, as in send word
i.e. abbreviates the Latin id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: A political communication swamps a distracted Republican.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone preoccupied has their mind taken up by anxiety, which is the state of being worried.

clue.text: Irrational idolatries — they are found near the front of this magazine

definitions.text: they are found near the front of this magazine

indicators.note: irrational suggests disordered thinking, so the letters of idolatries are set out in a new order

parts.note: the word idolatries supplies the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A jab at blind devotion, followed by a nod to the pages up front in The Nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The magazine is The Nation, where the puzzle appeared; its opinion pieces sit near the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Editorials are the opinion columns a magazine prints early in each issue.

clue.text: At first, Lebanese instrument is not subtle

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter of Lebanese is used

parts.note: the first letter of Lebanese is the one kept
the oud is a short-necked lute played across the Middle East

explanation.surface: A Lebanese instrument is described as anything but delicate.
explanation.definitionFit: Something brash and showy is called loud, the opposite of subtle.

clue.text: Anarchic roar incited true believer

indicators.note: anarchic means chaotic and lawless, so the letters of roar incited are thrown into disorder

parts.note: these two words supply the eleven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A chaotic howl stirs up a zealot.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctrinaire person follows a doctrine rigidly, a true believer who will not bend.

clue.text: I space out around wrong places to buy drugs

indicators.note: around means those scattered letters surround the word for wrong
out means the letters of I space are scattered into a new order

parts.note: these two words supply the six letters to be rearranged
harm means a wrong done to someone

explanation.surface: Someone spacing out near seedy spots where drugs are sold.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests illicit dealing; the definition is the innocent sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Pharmacies are shops that dispense medicines, legally.

clue.text: Cache rudimentary audio holding — that's clever

indicators.note: audio says to listen to the words as spoken rather than as spelt
holding says the spoken phrase contains the sound needed, which starts partway through it

parts.note: cache is said cash, and rude can mean primitive, a sense of rudimentary; the sh at the end of cash runs on into rude

explanation.surface: A hoard of basic sound equipment earns a compliment.
explanation.walkthrough: Say cash rude aloud: the sh ending of cash runs into rude, and that stretch of sound is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrewd move is an astute, sharp-witted one.

clue.text: Pitiful way to quote reactionary

parts.note: a path is a way

indicators.note: reactionary hints at going backwards, so the word for quote is turned round

parts.note: to cite is to quote

explanation.surface: A sad way of quoting a right-wing reactionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitiful and pathetic both describe something so poor it arouses pity or contempt.

clue.text: Secretly like film?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in private, a legal phrase for a hearing closed to the public
second meaning, literally: the way film sits inside a camera

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the literal reading: film is loaded into a camera.
explanation.definitionFit: In camera is a legal term for proceedings held in private, so it means secretly.

clue.text: Someone occupying the White House in the absence of chief occupant

indicators.note: in the absence of chief means the head letter of the White House occupant is dropped

parts.note: the US president lives in the White House

explanation.surface: A description of whoever lives in the White House when the boss is away.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half of the clue looks like the definition; the real one is the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident is someone living in a place, an occupant of it.

clue.text: E.g., Lisa and Paul entertaining an afterthought

indicators.note: entertaining means the singer's surname hosts the afterthought, holding it inside

parts.note: Paul Simon is the American singer-songwriter
PS, the postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter

explanation.surface: Two celebrities, Lisa and Paul, play host to a last-minute thought.
explanation.walkthrough: Lisa and Paul look like a pair; Lisa is the definition and Paul the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Lisa Simpson is the clever daughter in the cartoon The Simpsons.

clue.text: Communist skill backing Wall Street occupation

indicators.note: backing means the two words for communist and skill are put in reverse

parts.note: red is the traditional label for a communist
art means skill, as in the art of persuasion

explanation.surface: A communist with a knack supports the Occupy Wall Street protest.
explanation.walkthrough: Occupation looks like the protest of 2011; here it means a job, and the answer is the person who does it.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying and selling stocks is the classic Wall Street job, done by a trader.

clue.text: Head of senate departed, drawn and stooped

indicators.note: departed means that letter leaves the word for drawn

parts.note: a plan that is drawn is designed

indicators.note: head of means just the first letter of senate

parts.note: the opening letter of senate is the one removed

explanation.surface: A senate leader left the room looking haggard and bent.
explanation.walkthrough: Drawn and stooped read as a tired posture; drawn is wordplay and stooped means condescended.
explanation.definitionFit: To deign is to lower oneself to do something, which is to stoop to it.

clue.text: Public spectacle on the rise over the United States: a pain in the neck, mostly

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the first piece sits above the second
on the rise in a down clue means the letters read upwards, in reverse
mostly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a crick is a painful stiffness in the neck
US is the usual abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: A grand show rises over America, though it is something of an irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: A pain in the neck reads as a nuisance; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A circus is any noisy public show, and also the travelling entertainment itself.

clue.text: Tubers (potatoes) ultimately can come back

indicators.note: come back means the letters run in the opposite direction
ultimately means only the closing letter of potatoes is used

parts.note: the last letter of potatoes is the one kept
may and can both express permission

explanation.surface: Root vegetables, potatoes included, may finally return.
explanation.definitionFit: Yams are starchy tropical root crops, tubers like the potato.

clue.text: Occupancy that nuns undergo?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the act of living in a place
second meaning, whimsically: the process of putting on a habit, as nuns do

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke reading: a nun's robe is a habit, and -ation turns it into a process.
explanation.definitionFit: Habitation means dwelling in a place, which is occupancy; split differently it suggests dressing in a nun's garment.

clue.text: Occupied, like public transportation?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: engaged, having a lot to do
second meaning, whimsically: resembling a bus, read as bus plus -y

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the made-up adjective: something bus-like would be bus-y.
explanation.definitionFit: A busy person is occupied with tasks; split as bus plus y it suggests something bus-like.

clue.text: Nameless, leaderless throngs heralding recovery

indicators.note: heralding means the first piece comes before the second, announcing it
leaderless means the crowds lose their front letter

parts.note: mobs are throngs of people
a cure is a recovery from illness

explanation.surface: Anonymous crowds with no one in charge announce a comeback, a nod to the leaderless Occupy protests.
explanation.definitionFit: An obscure person is little known, without a name anyone recognises.

clue.text: On beginning, antonyms affront

parts.note: off is the opposite of on
end is the opposite of beginning

explanation.surface: Someone finds words with opposite meanings insulting from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: Antonyms tells you to replace each of the first two words with its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: To affront someone is to insult them openly, which is to offend.

clue.text: In Tuscany, who opposed wine?

parts.note: chi is the Italian word for who, and Tuscany is in Italy
anti means opposed to

explanation.surface: An Italian asks which of them was against the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Chianti is the red wine made in the hills of Tuscany.

clue.text: Fops take a shine to Aykroyd and Rather

parts.note: to fancy someone is to take a shine to them
the comic actor Dan Aykroyd and the news anchor Dan Rather are both Dans

explanation.surface: Dandies grow fond of a comedian and a television newsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A fancy dan is a showy, vain person, the same type as a fop.

clue.text: Move sneakily, occupying business I'd leveraged

indicators.note: occupying says the answer sits inside the phrase business I'd leveraged, taking up part of it

parts.note: the answer runs from the end of business through I'd into leveraged

explanation.surface: Someone slips quietly into a leveraged business deal.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidle is to edge along furtively, a sneaky way of moving.
